item.title: How to stop saying 'Fuck you Cursor'
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 9 (thread link) | @sbpayne
December 14, 2024 | https://skylarbpayne.com/posts/cursed-cursor | archive.org

or How to Stop Fighting with your AI Pair Programmer

Cursor agent is worse than old composer.

Might go back to previous version
@ codebase

— Riley Brown (@rileybrown_ai) December 3, 2024

As someone who’s led multiple engineering teams build products from inception to international launch, I’ve seen this reaction countless times. Engineers get excited about AI coding assistants, try them out, and then… frustration. The tool seems to fight against them at every turn.

But here’s the truth I’ve learned after months of using Cursor daily while leading engineering teams and shipping production ML systems: the problem isn’t the AI. It’s how we work with it.

The Real Problem: You’re Working Solo in a Pair Programming World

Nick Dobos recently tweeted about Cursor’s agent mode:

Yoo @cursor_ai agent is CRAZY

The new ai agent mode can call arbitrary python functions in your code base!!

This means you can tell cursor agent to build its own tools!!!

“Build be a python function that can search the web”. “Now call that function to search for …” 🤯 https://t.co/gQV7qOilXu

— Nick Dobos (@NickADobos) November 27, 2024

He’s right - it is powerful. But that power is precisely why so many developers get frustrated. When you give an eager junior developer access to your entire codebase without proper guidance, what happens? The same thing that happens with Cursor’s agent mode.

As Cole Murray insightfully noted:

The people who are complaining AI sucks and doesn’t generate what they want

🤝

The people who are complaining their direct reports don’t do what they want.

Maybe you’re just bad at communicating what you want.

— cole murray (@_colemurray) December 11, 2024

In this guide, I’ll share the concrete workflow I’ve developed that transformed Cursor from a source of frustration into a genuine productivity multiplier. You’ll learn:

  • A structured approach to working with Cursor’s agent
  • How to handle both greenfield development and existing codebases
  • Complete configuration files and templates you can use today
  • Real examples from production systems

Most importantly, you’ll learn how to stop fighting with your AI pair programmer and start collaborating effectively.

The Core Problem: Communication

When using Cursor, many developers (myself included, initially) are still in a solo development mindset while technically pair programming with AI. We give one-line instructions and expect perfect implementation. Would you do that with a human teammate, particularly a junior engineer?

The solution? Treat Cursor as a teammate, not a god.

Working “Alone” Together

The irony of AI programming tools is that while they’re meant to enhance collaboration, most developers use them as if they’re still working alone. Have you ever found yourself:

# Dropping a massive chunk of code into Cursor with just:
"Fix this code"

# Or giving vague, one-line requirements like:
"Write me a function to process user data"

# Or worse, expecting it to understand complex context without explanation:
"Update this to handle the new requirements"

This approach is particularly problematic with Cursor’s agent mode, which can make sweeping changes across your codebase if not properly guided. It’s like having an eager intern with access to your entire codebase but no understanding of your team’s conventions or system architecture.

The One-Line Instruction Anti-Pattern

Let’s look at a typical interaction that leads to frustration:

Developer: "Add error handling to this function"

Cursor: *Proceeds to rewrite entire function, adding try-catch blocks everywhere, 
        changing variable names for "clarity", and introducing new helper functions*

Developer: "No, that's not what I wanted!"

Cursor: *Suggests another complete rewrite with different error handling patterns*

Developer: "F**k you Cursor!"

This pattern is especially dangerous when working with existing codebases. Cursor’s agent eagerly tries to “improve” code it sees, often breaking subtle but important patterns that aren’t immediately obvious.

Why This Fails

The failure modes become even more apparent when we compare this to human collaboration:

With a Junior Developer

You: "Here's a task. Add error handling to this function."
Junior Dev: "Okay, what kind of errors should we handle?"
You: "Good question. We need to catch network timeouts and invalid data formats."
Junior Dev: "Got it. Should we use our standard error types?"
You: "Yes, and make sure to log the errors with our logging framework."

With Cursor (Common Approach)

You: "Add error handling to this function"
Cursor: *Makes massive changes*
You: *Frustration intensifies*

The problem isn’t that Cursor is incapable - it’s that we’re not providing the same level of context and guidance we would to a human teammate.

This problem compounds when working with existing code. Consider these common scenarios:

  1. Hidden Dependencies

    # Cursor sees:
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)
   
# What it doesn't see:
# - transform() has side effects
# - Other services depend on the exact output format
# - Performance requirements that aren't obvious

  2. Implicit Patterns

    # Your codebase consistently uses:
try:
    result = risky_operation()
except SpecificError as e:
    logger.error(f"Operation failed: {e}")
    raise OperationalError(e)
   
# Cursor might introduce:
try:
    result = risky_operation()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")  # Breaking logging patterns
    return None  # Breaking error handling patterns

  3. Testing Implications

    # Cursor changes a function signature:
def process(data, config=None):  # Added optional parameter
       
# But doesn't realize this breaks:
# - Hundred of tests expecting specific behavior
# - API contracts with other services
# - Serialization/deserialization logic

The Root Cause

The fundamental issue is treating AI as a magic code generator rather than a collaborative team member. When we:

  • Skip proper requirement discussions
  • Don’t provide necessary context
  • Fail to review changes incrementally
  • Don’t explain our codebase’s patterns and constraints

We’re setting ourselves up for frustration. Just as you wouldn’t expect a new team member to write perfect code without proper onboarding, you shouldn’t expect Cursor to do so without proper guidance.

In the next section, we’ll look at a better way: a structured workflow that treats Cursor as a proper development partner rather than a god.

A Better Way: Structured Collaboration

The Four-Phase Workflow

After months of trial and error leading engineering teams through AI-assisted development, I’ve distilled our process into four key phases. This isn’t just another software development lifecycle - it’s specifically designed for effective AI collaboration while maintaining engineering rigor.

  1. Problem Statement & Requirements
    • Start with open discussion of the problem space
    • Work through expectations until you reach shared understanding
    • Document key constraints and acceptance criteria
    • Goal: Clear alignment before any code is written
  2. Design Documentation
    • Create a structured design document (I use a standard template)
    • Review and iterate on the design with Cursor
    • Break implementation into clear phases
    • Goal: Roadmap that both you and Cursor understand
  3. Phased Implementation
    • Implement solution in planned phases
    • Always reference back to the design doc
    • Regular validation against requirements
    • Goal: Manageable, reviewable chunks of work
  4. Continuous Testing
    • Follow testing strategy for each phase
    • Mix automated tests with manual validation
    • Ensure backwards compatibility
    • Goal: Confidence in changes

Key Principles

What makes this workflow effective?

  1. Small, Verifiable Steps

    # Instead of:
"Add error handling to the entire codebase"
   
# Do:
"Let's first identify the critical paths that need error handling"
"For the data processing function, what specific errors should we catch?"
"How should we integrate with our existing logging system?"

  2. Clear Context Boundaries

    # Instead of:
"Make this code better"
   
# Do:
"We need to improve error handling in process_data() to:
 1. Catch network timeouts (currently unhandled)
 2. Log errors using our standard format
 3. Maintain the existing retry behavior
 4. Keep the current function signature"

  3. Iterative Refinement

    # Instead of fighting multiple changes:
"No, not like that... no, that's not right either..."
   
# Have a dialogue:
"Good start. Let's adjust the error types to match our standards."
"Now let's add the logging integration."
"Finally, let's add the retry mechanism."

Real-World Example: Version Checksums

In the next sections, I’ll walk through a complete example of using this workflow to add version checksums to an email reply agent system. You’ll see how we:

  1. Started with a clear problem statement
  2. Developed a comprehensive design document
  3. Implemented the solution in phases
  4. Added robust testing

This wasn’t a theoretical exercise - it was a real feature we needed to prevent configuration drift in our multi-agent system. By following this structured approach, we were able to implement it correctly the first time, with no production incidents.

Initial Problem Statement

Let’s see how this workflow plays out in practice. We’ll start with discussing requirements - notice how each response builds on the previous one, creating a shared understanding.

Me: Currently, there's no way to detect if an agent's configuration has changed without a corresponding version bump. This could lead to inconsistent behavior where the same version number refers to different agent configurations. How can we detect this? Do not write code, just discuss the problem.

Cursor: You're right! There is no way to detect if an agent's configuration has changed without a corresponding version bump. We can use a checksum of the agent's configuration to detect changes. Would you like me to implement this?

Me: Let's discuss some requirements first to make sure we have the same understanding. Do not write code, just discuss the problem. First, when trying to create a new agent version which already exists, but is somehow different, we should raise an error. We don't need to get fancy and "auto update" the version number right now. The checksum should be deterministic and consistent, obviously to do this check. The check should not be performance critical; but considering most of the time is spent in the LLM inference, it is okay for it to take a little bit of time (e.g. time for a database transatction). We want to maintain backward compatibility with existing agent versions where we did not store the checksum. When there is a mismatch, we should have a clear error message. Anything else you think we should consider?

Cursor: Checksum Scope
What exactly should be included in the checksum calculation?
Should we include runtime dependencies versions?
Should we include tool implementations or just tool names?
How do we handle dynamic components (like system prompts that might depend on runtime state)?
Storage Considerations
Since we're using SQLModel, should the checksum be stored or always computed?
If stored, how do we handle migrations for existing records?
If computed, do we need indexing for efficient lookups?
3. Error Handling
Should we provide details about what changed in the error message?
Do we need different error types for different kinds of mismatches?
How do we handle validation failures during bulk operations?
Validation Timing
When exactly should we perform the validation?
Should we validate on every agent instantiation or just during version creation?
How do we handle validation in async contexts?
Debugging Support
Should we provide tools to inspect/compare checksums?
How do we help users understand why a checksum changed?
Should we log checksum computations for audit purposes?

Me: We should include runtime dependencies. Tool names are sufficient for now. No dynamic components for now, let's keep it simple. I think the checksum should be computed; because it is a derived attirbute; that makes it easier to change later, and also makes backwards compatibility simple. The data for now will be small; no indexing required. No need for now to determine what changed. In most cases, the right thing to do will be to just bump the version number. One error type should suffice. There are currently no bulk operations on agent_versions. The validation should be performed on every agent version creation. Use transactions to ensure correctness in async contexts. No need to create tools to inspect/compare checksums for now. Please summarize your understanding of the problem and requirements before we continue.

Cursor: Problem Statement:
We need to prevent silent configuration drift in agent versions. Currently, an agent's configuration could be modified without changing its version number, leading to inconsistent behavior. We need a way to detect these changes and enforce version updates.
Core Requirements:
Detect configuration changes by computing a deterministic checksum of the agent's configuration
Raise an error if trying to create an agent version that exists but has different configuration
Users should manually bump version numbers when configurations change
Technical Decisions:
Checksum includes: static configuration + tool names + runtime dependencies
Implemented as a computed property (not stored in database)
Single error type with clear message
Validation happens during agent version creation
Use database transactions for async safety
Keep implementation simple (no inspection tools, bulk operations, or change detection)
Non-Requirements (for now):
No automatic version bumping
No dynamic components in checksum
No tool implementation checksums
No inspection/comparison tools
No indexing for checksums
No detailed change detection

While this might seem like a lot of detail upfront – it’s all important stuff to make sure Cursor is going to do the right thing! Now let’s make a design doc!

Design Document

Me: Let's create a design document given the problem statement and requirements we discussed. Please write a markdown file following the @context/design_doc.md template.

And Cursor drops this gold on us:

# Agent Version Checksum Feature

## Problem Statement

We need to prevent silent configuration drift in agent versions. When an agent's 
configuration is modified without changing its version number, it can lead to:

- Inconsistent behavior between environments
- Hard to debug issues
- Loss of reproducibility
- Untracked configuration changes

## Requirements

### Functional Requirements

- Compute deterministic checksum of agent configuration
- Validate configuration matches when creating agent versions
- Raise error if version exists with different configuration
- Support existing agent versions (backward compatibility)

### Non-Functional Requirements

- Performance: Can tolerate database transaction overhead
- Clear error messages directing users to bump version
- Simple implementation (single error type)
- Safe operation in async contexts

## Design Decisions

### 1. Checksum Storage

Implemented as computed field because:

- Easier to modify checksum logic later
- Simplifies backward compatibility
- Keeps data model clean
- Reflects derived nature of the field

### 2. Checksum Algorithm

Uses SHA-256 because:

- Cryptographically secure (prevents accidental collisions)
- Standard library implementation available
- Fast computation
- Widely used and trusted

### 3. Configuration Serialization

Uses deterministic JSON serialization because:

- Handles nested configurations naturally
- Human-readable for debugging
- Consistent across Python versions
- Supports all needed data types

### 4. Checksum Scope

Includes in computation:

- Static configuration
- Tool names (not implementations)
- Runtime dependencies

Excludes:

- Dynamic components
- Tool implementations
- Runtime state

## Technical Design

### 1. Core Components

```python
class AgentVersion:
    """Stores and validates agent version information"""
    version: str
    checksum: str
    
    def validate_checksum(self, config: AgentConfig) -> bool:
        """Validates configuration matches stored checksum"""
        return self.checksum == compute_checksum(config)

def compute_checksum(config: AgentConfig) -> str:
    """Generates deterministic checksum from configuration"""
    serialized = json.dumps(config.dict(), sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()
```

### 2. Integration Points

- AgentVersion integrates with InstrumentedAgent creation
- Validation occurs during agent initialization
- Checksum computation hooks into configuration serialization
- Error handling integrates with agent creation workflow

## Implementation Plan

1. Phase 1: Core Implementation (Completed)
   - Added checksum field to AgentVersion
   - Implemented checksum computation
   - Added validation logic
   - Created error types

2. Phase 2: Migration (Completed)
   - Updated existing agent configurations
   - Added validation to agent creation
   - Updated tests
   - Added documentation

## Testing Strategy

### Unit Tests

- Checksum computation consistency
- Version validation logic
- Configuration change detection
- Error case handling

### Integration Tests

- Agent creation workflow
- Configuration updates
- Version management
- Migration scenarios

## Observability

### Logging

- Configuration validation results
- Checksum computation details
- Version mismatch events
- Migration progress

### Metrics

- Validation failures
- Configuration changes
- Version updates
- Migration status

## Future Considerations

### Potential Enhancements

- Version comparison operations
- Configuration drift detection
- Automated version bumping
- Checksum verification tools

### Known Limitations

- Only detects changes in serializable fields
- Requires manual version management
- No partial configuration updates
- Limited to JSON-serializable types

## Dependencies

### Runtime Dependencies

- Python standard library (json, hashlib)
- Existing agent configuration system
- Version management system

### Development Dependencies

- Testing framework
- JSON schema validation
- Development documentation

## Security Considerations

- Checksum algorithm is cryptographically secure
- No sensitive data in checksums
- Version records are immutable
- Validation prevents configuration tampering

## Rollout Strategy

1. Development phase (Completed)
   - Core implementation
   - Test coverage
   - Documentation

2. Testing phase (Completed)
   - Unit tests
   - Integration tests
   - Migration testing

3. Production deployment (Completed)
   - Gradual rollout
   - Migration support
   - Monitoring

## References

- Original design document
- Agent configuration documentation
- Version management system documentation
- SHA-256 specification

This design document gives us clear boundaries for implementation while remaining flexible enough for iteration. Note how it includes concrete interfaces and clear phase definitions. I can hear you already: “BuT cUrSoR hAlLuCiNaTeS!” Totally! And that’s why we need to review and verify the work. We are FORCING Cursor to output enough information so that we can verify. How closely you pay attention to certain details is mostly a function of your risk tolerance. Everything you do not carefully verify is something that could be wrong – just like with a human teammate you are mentoring! Not meant as a slight to the human teammate, they are learning; everyone has to start somewhere.

I like this design, except that it isn’t properly using SQLModel as it should, let’s remind Cursor of that for the interfaces:

Me: Let's amend this design document. Keep in mind we should be using SQLModel for storage of the fields. I think we should use `@hybrid_property` from SQLAlchemy to make it storable in the database.

And it updated the interface to this (looks good to me):

class AgentVersion(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Stores and validates agent version information"""
    # Primary key fields
    agent_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    version_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    
    # Metadata
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    
    # Configuration fields (stored as JSON)
    prompt_template: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    tools: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    runtime_info: dict[str, str] = Field(default={}, sa_column=Column(JSON))
    
    @hybrid_property
    def checksum(self) -> str:
        """Compute checksum from static fields."""
        static_fields = {
            "prompt_template": self.prompt_template,
            "tools": sorted(self.tools),
            "runtime_info": self.runtime_info,
        }
        serialized = json.dumps(static_fields, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()

One thing I’ll admit here: this wasn’t entirely generated by Cursor. I made one hand edit. And that’s okay! I added the sorted(self.tools) to ensure the order of tools is consistent. This was easier to do myself than explain to the AI.

Now we have a good looking design doc, let’s move on to the implementation!

Implementation and Testing

Now, we are all familiar with the cyclic and iterative nature of implementation and testing. You try something, it doesn’t work, you try something else. Rinse and repeat. It’s no different here! Let’s start with the first phase of implementation and testing. Remember: we ALWAYS refer to back to the previous step to “ground” Cursor.

Me: Please implement the first phase of @design/agent_version_checksum.md.

Cursor then starts by creating a new branch:

git checkout -b feature/agent-version-checksum-phase-1

And then Cursor excitedly starts writing code. It’s challenging to show all the code that was written because some were edits, but suffice to say: Cursor was pretty damn close to the design document. The key implementation in phase 1 was this:

class AgentVersion(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Captures the complete configuration of an agent at a point in time."""

    __table__: ClassVar[Table]

    version_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    agent_id: str = Field(index=True)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    prompt_template: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    tools: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    runtime_info: dict[str, str] = Field(default={}, sa_column=Column(JSON))

    @hybrid_property
    def checksum(self) -> str:
        """Compute checksum of static configuration fields."""
        static_fields = {
            "prompt_template": self.prompt_template,
            "tools": sorted(self.tools),
        }
        serialized = json.dumps(static_fields, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()
   
   def validate_configuration(self, agent_config: "AgentConfig") -> None:
        """Validate that an agent config matches this version's configuration.
        
        Args:
            agent_config: The configuration to validate
            
        Raises:
            ConfigurationError: If the configuration doesn't match this version
        """
        # Convert agent config to comparable format
        config_prompt = [agent_config.system_prompt]
        config_tools = sorted(getattr(agent_config, 'tools', []))
        
        check_fields = {
            "prompt_template": config_prompt,
            "tools": config_tools,
        }
        
        check_sum = hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(check_fields, sort_keys=True).encode()
        ).hexdigest()
        
        if check_sum != self.checksum:
            raise ConfigurationError(
                f"Configuration mismatch for version {self.version_id}. "
                f"Expected checksum {self.checksum}, got {check_sum}. "
                "Did you forget to bump the version number?"
            )

I generally like to start with a sort of manual e2e test when I am working on smaller projects.

Me: Please run the agent to ensure nothing is broken.

Cursor suggests running the following: uv run -m email_reply_agent.gmail_agent And we quickly find that the agent is broken!

pydantic.errors.PydanticUserError: A non-annotated attribute was detected: `checksum = <sqlalchemy.ext.hybrid.hybrid_property object at 0x1058058d0>`. All model fields require a type annotation; if `checksum` is not meant to be a field, you may be able to resolve this error by annotating it as a `ClassVar` or updating `model_config['ignored_types']`.

It appears that the agent is broken, and it has something to do with the new checksum attribute. As most people do, we pipe that error back to Cursor, Cursor makes another edit, and then we run the agent again… Same error! Now here is where we usually get frustrated, Cursor obviously is stuck and does not know what to do. Cursor is a nervous intern! They don’t want to admit they don’t know; we need to help by providing context.

A quick Google search from me shows that @hybrid_property is not the way to use a computed field in SQLModel (oopsie my bad), instead we should use @computed_field! I provide that as context, using Hamel’s awesome chrome extension to convert a webpage to markdown. I also told Cursor I didn’t like having a “validate” method in the class and would prefer inlining the comparison, and Cursor made the change:

class AgentVersion(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Captures the complete configuration of an agent at a point in time."""

    # Use SQLAlchemy Table for proper table configuration
    __table__: ClassVar[Table]

    agent_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    version_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    prompt_template: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    tools: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    runtime_info: dict[str, str] = Field(default={}, sa_column=Column(JSON))

    @computed_field
    @property
    def checksum(self) -> str:
        """Compute checksum from static fields."""
        static_fields = {
            "prompt_template": self.prompt_template,
            "tools": sorted(self.tools),
            "runtime_info": self.runtime_info,
        }
        serialized = json.dumps(static_fields, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()

    class Config: # type: ignore  # noqa: PGH003
        table = True
        arbitrary_types_allowed = True

    # Set table name after class definition
    __tablename__ = "agent_versions" # type: ignore  # noqa: PGH003

...

async def store_version(self, version: AgentVersion) -> None:
        """Store an agent version if it doesn't exist.

        Args:
            version: The version to store

        Raises:
            ConfigurationError: If version exists with different configuration
        """
        async with self.db.session() as session:
            # Check if version exists
            stmt = select(AgentVersion).where(
                and_(
                    AgentVersion.agent_id == version.agent_id,
                    AgentVersion.version_id == version.version_id,
                )
            )
            existing = await session.execute(stmt)
            existing_version = existing.scalar_one_or_none()

            if existing_version is not None:
                if existing_version.checksum != version.checksum:
                    raise ConfigurationError(  # noqa: TRY003
                        f"Configuration mismatch for agent {version.agent_id} "
                        f"version {version.version_id}. "
                        "The configuration has changed without a version bump."
                    )
                return  # Version exists and matches

            session.add(version)
            await session.commit()

And this code worked! It ran successfully the first time, then when I changed the config without the version, it failed!

Then we ask Cursor to write a few unit tests to ensure the checksum is computed correctly:

Me: Okay, the manual run is working. Now let's write a few unit tests to ensure the checksum is computed correctly.

Cursor writes a few unit tests, and we run them to ensure they pass:

"""Tests for agent version checksum functionality."""
import pytest
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlmodel import SQLModel

from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.models import AgentVersion
from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.storage import SQLModelStorage, ConfigurationError


@pytest.fixture
async def db_session():
    """Create a test database session."""
    engine = create_async_engine(
        "sqlite+aiosqlite:///test.db",
        echo=False,
    )
    
    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)
    
    async_session = sessionmaker(
        engine, class_=AsyncSession, expire_on_commit=False
    )
    
    async with async_session() as session:
        yield session
        await session.rollback()
    
    await engine.dispose()


@pytest.fixture
def storage(db_session):
    """Create a test storage instance."""
    return SQLModelStorage(db_session)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_checksum_computation():
    """Test that checksum is computed correctly."""
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # Same config should have same checksum
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    assert version.checksum == version2.checksum

    # Different config should have different checksum
    version3 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    assert version.checksum != version3.checksum


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_storage_validation(storage):
    """Test that version storage validates checksums."""
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # First store should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Same version should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Different config with same version should fail
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    with pytest.raises(ConfigurationError):
        await storage.store_version(version2)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_order_independence():
    """Test that checksum is independent of field order."""
    version1 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9", "os": "linux"}
    )
    
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool2", "tool1"],  # Different order
        runtime_info={"os": "linux", "python": "3.9"}  # Different order
    )
    
    assert version1.checksum == version2.checksum

uv run pytest tests/test_agent_version_checksum.py

But we find a failure:

================================================================================= short test summary info =================================================================================
ERROR tests/test_agent_version_checksum.py::test_version_storage_validation - AttributeError: 'async_generator' object has no attribute 'database_url'
========================================================================= 2 passed, 2 warnings, 1 error in 0.13s ==========================================================================

So we tell Cursor to fix the test. Key insight here: don’t just jump into fixing the test, but instead think about and discuss the problem with me!

Me: One test failed with: ERROR tests/test_agent_version_checksum.py::test_version_storage_validation - AttributeError: 'async_generator' object has no attribute 'database_url'. Please discuss the problem and how you think we can fix it. Do not write code.

Cursor: Ah, I see the issue. The problem is with our test fixture setup. The storage fixture is receiving the session directly, but SQLModelStorage expects a database configuration object with a session factory method. Would you like me to fix the test?

Me: Yes, that sounds right, please proceed! Make a separate SQLModelConfig fixture that we can use to configure and setup the database.

Then Cursor makes a fix:

"""Tests for agent version checksum functionality."""
import pytest
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlmodel import SQLModel

from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.models import AgentVersion
from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.storage import ConfigurationError, SQLModelConfig, SQLModelStorage


@pytest.fixture
def storage_config():
    return SQLModelConfig(
        database_url="sqlite+aiosqlite:///test.db",
        echo=False
    )


async def setup_database(storage_config):
    """Set up and tear down the test database."""
    print("Setting up database:", storage_config.database_url)
    engine = create_async_engine(
        storage_config.database_url,
        echo=False
    )

    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        print("Creating all tables:", SQLModel.metadata.tables)
        await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)


@pytest.fixture
def storage(storage_config):
    """Create a test storage instance."""
    return SQLModelStorage(storage_config)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_checksum_computation():
    """Test that checksum is computed correctly."""
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # Same config should have same checksum
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    assert version.checksum == version2.checksum

    # Different config should have different checksum
    version3 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    assert version.checksum != version3.checksum


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_storage_validation(storage, storage_config):
    """Test that version storage validates checksums."""
    await setup_database(storage_config)
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # First store should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Same version should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Different config with same version should fail
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    with pytest.raises(ConfigurationError):
        await storage.store_version(version2)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_order_independence():
    """Test that checksum is independent of field order."""
    version1 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9", "os": "linux"}
    )
    
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool2", "tool1"],  # Different order
        runtime_info={"os": "linux", "python": "3.9"}  # Different order
    )
    
    assert version1.checksum == version2.checksum

Now I am pretty happy with the implementation and the tests pass. One thing that bothers me is that the test.db is not cleaned up here:

Me: Please make sure in @test_agent_version_checksum.py that we clean up the database in between test runs.

Cursor makes a fix and now the tests pass and the database is cleaned up! I’m pretty happy:

class TestDatabase:
    """Context manager for test database setup and cleanup."""
    
    def __init__(self, config: SQLModelConfig):
        self.config = config
        self.engine = create_async_engine(config.database_url, echo=False)
    
    async def __aenter__(self):
        """Create database tables."""
        async with self.engine.begin() as conn:
            await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)
    
    async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        """Drop database tables and cleanup."""
        async with self.engine.begin() as conn:
            await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.drop_all)
        await self.engine.dispose()

# ... then in tests

async with TestDatabase(storage_config):
   ...


Me: Please make a PR for the first phase of @design/agent_version_checksum.md.

Cursor runs the following commands:

git add .
git commit -m "First phase of agent version checksum"
gh pr create --title "First phase of agent version checksum" --body "First phase of agent version checksum"

And I can then go review the PR, and merge it!

Best Practices

Now that we have gone through a full cycle of this workflow, I want to extract out what I have found to be best practices.

  • Enforce an opinionated development workflow on Cursor: the specific workflow I went through is not necessarily a best practice; it’s that I went through a workflow that’s the highest leverage. Adapt to your own setting as needed!
  • Focus on collaboration and communication before code: Cursor (and sometimes we) are so eager to jump into code. But before we really understand that’s a mistake! Give explicit “Do not write code” directives.
  • Always force Cursor to use the context of the previous step: this helps ground Cursor to the most recent item you agreed on. It’s important to “attach” the resource to the context of your conversation too. Because you may have made edits Cursor didn’t see!
  • Limit the Size of Each Step: don’t give Cursor too much to chew on at once. This is a great way to get stuck in a loop. Instead, give them smaller chunks (this is why I split up the design doc into phases).
  • Guide the Discussion: without guardrails, Cursor will… well go off the rails. Make sure to keep Cursor on track. Don’t be afraid to “cancel” Cursor and reset.
  • Return to the Previous Step if Needed: sometimes Cursor will seem hopelessly stuck in a loop. Don’t keep going forward; go backwards. It is clear that Cursor is missing (or misunderstanding) some critical context; discuss what that is before proceeding (and make according edits to artifacts like design docs)!
  • Document Everything: Force Cursor (and yourself) to leave breadcrumbs. This will help you pick up where you left off and be critical for you, Cursor, and possibly other teammates to understand what’s going on!

Tips for Applying in Teams

Engineering leaders constantly tell me: “oh I can use Cursor because I know what I’m doing, but the junior engineers really can’t use it effectively”. I think this is bullshit. The reality is that this is a tool like any other, and it is the responsibility of senior engineers / leaders to teach juniors how to use their tools effectively. AI does not let senior engineers off the hook for mentoring their juniors. And we also should be cautious about giving junior engineers too much for them to chew.

Here is what I found worked best:

  • Give smaller chunks: instead of giving a junior the entire project from the start, do the first few steps with them. Then you can hand off a design doc and let them take a stab at implementing whatever “phase 1” is.
  • Review intermediate phases: if you give a junior a design doc, you should review their implementation of the first phase. This will help you understand their level of understanding and give you a chance to guide them. But you could also give them the entire project upfront and review each step – e.g. review the problem statement / requirements upfront. This can be an incredible way to help them grow!
  • Give more complex tasks as they grow: as the junior grows, you can increase the complexity of what you give them (and of what you let them do).
  • Regularly pair with them: I have never found a good substitute for sitting down and pairing with them; you get a lot of insight into how they think and what may unlock their growth.

From Fighting to Flow: Making AI Work For You

When I started working with AI coding tools, I experienced the same frustrations you might be feeling now. But after leading multiple teams to successfully integrate these tools into their workflows, I’ve seen firsthand how transformative they can be when used effectively.

The key shift? Stop treating AI as a code generation oracle and start treating it as a collaborative team member. The workflow I’ve shared isn’t just theory – it’s battle-tested across multiple international product launches and production ML systems.

Remember:

  • A structured workflow beats raw capability
  • Clear communication prevents most problems
  • Small, focused steps lead to better outcomes
  • Teams grow stronger when given the right framework

Ready to Transform Your AI Development?

If you want to dive deeper:

  • Check out my Cursor setup guide for technical configuration
  • Connect with me on LinkedIn to discuss AI development practices
  • Follow me on X for daily insights on effective AI collaboration
  • Schedule a consultation if you need help building an AI-powered development workflow for your team

Most importantly, start small. Pick one project, apply this workflow, and adjust it to your needs. You’ll be surprised how quickly fighting with your AI assistant turns into flowing with a capable teammate.

Share your experiences with me on X or LinkedIn – I’d love to hear how this workflow works for you and what you’ve learned along the way.

item.title: Why Emacs Is the Best: 10 Key Advantages
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @ossusermivami
December 14, 2024 | https://midirus.com/blog/emacs-30 | archive.org

In this post I explain why I believe Emacs is the greatest text editor.

You can find my configuration here: emacs.el. It is a light standalone file that setups a minimal developer environment with auto completion, projects management, language server and some quality of life improvements.

Context

I recently setup a new developer environment from scratch. I started with the emacs-nox package, which is the lightweight terminal edition without the graphic libraries. Then, I progressively setup the configurations I needed. Before activating a new setting, I read through the documentation and the source code to refresh my memory. In a couple of days, I got Emacs working exactly as I wanted, and I was blown away by how far it has come.

Emacs is my main tool to create projects, contribute code, run experiments, read mail, and perform basically any text based activity. I would say it is my most valuable tool because over time I built a custom workflow that would be hard to replace with another tool. In the following section, I present how I use Emacs.

Features

In this section I present the main features I get with Emacs.

Completion framework

This key capability enhances the process of finding an element within a list. Emacs includes ido by default, but there are more advanced package available, such as vertico or ivy.

The concept is to use fuzzy matching to efficiently narrow down a list of elements. For instance, typing butler .hs will match entries containing both butler and .hs regardless of their order. Adding further keywords, like parser, further refines the list to only include entries with parser.

Emacs’s completion framework is pervasive and integrated into many systems, such as:

  • Finding a file,
  • Selecting a remote reference,
  • Executing a command.

Once you become accustomed to a robust completion system, it’s hard to go back.

Buffers

Emacs manages window content through objects called buffers, and switching between these buffers is a command I use frequently. Combined with recentf to track visited files and saveplace to restore the last cursor position, Emacs offers a fast and efficient system for recalling files.

When working on distributed systems with multiple projects, I often need to switch contexts, for example to alternate between a frontend application and a configuration management system. Over time I’ve accumulated over a thousand checkouts, and with just a few keystrokes, I can quickly access any project’s files:

  • project-switch-project loads a project from the list of checkout.
  • project-find-file selects a file within the current project.

Company

Company is a modular text completion framework that provides basic auto-completion for local paths, keywords, and abbreviations. It can be extended by other packages to enable custom completion, such as those provided by a language server.

Company is incredibly lightweight and operates seamlessly in the background. Its presence is so unobtrusive that I only notice it when it’s not there.

Elisp

Emacs is highly extensible through Lisp, a powerful and intriguing programming language. At a minimum, you only need to understand how to set variables and call functions to customize your environment: 

(setq recentf-max-saved-items 1024)
(recentf-mode)

From the editor, you can access the documentation and the sources of everything through the describe-* family of commands.

Then you can implement any kind of customization, for example, here is how to start a language server inside a nix shell when a flake is available: 

(defun start-hls (_mode)
  "Start HLS by trying to wrap in nix develop."
  (if (file-exists-p "flake.nix")
    (progn
      (message "Running HLS with flake")
      (list "nix" "develop" "--command" "haskell-language-server-wrapper" "--lsp"))
    (progn
      (message "Running HLS from host")
      (list "haskell-language-server-wrapper" "--lsp"))))

(add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs '(haskell-mode . start-hls))

Here is how I insert my latest screen capture into a markdown file: 

(defun get-newest-file-from-dir  (path)
  "Return the latest file in PATH."
  (car (directory-files path 'full nil #'file-newer-than-file-p)))

(defun copy-screenshot-markdown (name)
  "Move the latest screenshot and insert markdown link with NAME."
  (interactive "Mname: ")
  (let* ((infile (expand-file-name (get-newest-file-from-dir "~/Pictures/Screenshots")))
         (outdir (concat (file-name-directory (buffer-file-name)) "/media"))
         (outfile (expand-file-name (concat name ".png") outdir)))
    (unless (file-directory-p outdir) (make-directory outdir t))
    (rename-file infile outfile)
    (insert (concat "![" name "](media/" (file-name-nondirectory outfile) ")"))
    (newline)
    (newline)))

If you have never used Lisp, do yourself a favor and give it try, for example through this elisp-guide.

While Lisp isn’t my favorite language, I find it quite enjoyable to use, especially within the integrated environment that Emacs provides. I believe Lisp is a crucial factor in Emacs’s success and versatility.

Compilation

Emacs comes with a simple, yet powerful compilation mode that works like this:

  • compile, starts the build process by selecting a command like make.
  • next-error, jumps to the location of the next error according to compilation-error-regexp.
  • recompile, restarts the compilation process.

This workflow provides the ideal feedback loop to fix compilation errors.

Eglot

Emacs comes with a language server client called eglot that works like this:

  • eglot, start the language server.
  • eglot-shutdown, kill the server.
  • eglot-code-actions, execute server actions.
  • flymake-show-project-diagnostics, show the annotations.
  • xref-find-definitions, find definition.
  • xref-find-references, find call sites.

Eglot works seamlessly right out of the box, requiring no additional configuration or external packages. It’s impressive how it integrates with existing Emacs features like Flymake and Xref, which can also work without a language server, such as when using a standalone linter or TAGS.

Shell

Emacs can interact with inferior commands through a regular buffer. This works like a standard terminal but with the added benefit of text manipulation features. The main difference is that, instead of using the up arrow to scroll through shell history, you use M-p to access previous commands. It takes a little time to adjust to this, but the advantages of integrating a terminal within a text editor are significant:

  • You can select and copy output as you would with regular text using standard commands.
  • The buffer can be edited, allowing you to correct mistakes and create a polished transcript.

By running shells within Emacs, I can also implement a per project command history with my project-shell.el package.

Magit

Magit is a Git porcelain. It is such a major package I won’t introduce it here, checkout its website: https://magit.vc/. However, I would like to describe a key workflow for me:

  • In a diff, pressing enter visit the thing-at-point.
  • When the cursor is on a removed chunk, magit creates a temporary buffer to show the file’s previous version.
  • This temporary buffer works with other magit command like magit-blame.

Magit allows you to explore Git history effortlessly, handling the complex details transparently and seamlessly.

Org mode

Org is a powerful, outline-based notes management and organizer tool. If you’re not familiar with it yet, checkout its website for more details: https://orgmode.org/.

Combined with org-capture and org-agenda, it provides a fast and effective plain text system for getting things done. I previously introduced a project management system in this post, and recently, I developed the gnome-org-next-schedule extension to display my next scheduled task.

Notmuch

Notmuch is a fast, tag-based email system with powerful global search capabilities. It leverages the Xapian search engine library and features a user-friendly Emacs client. Notmuch handles millions of mails effortlessly, making it particularly well-suited for high-traffic development mailing lists. I’ve developed a custom workflow using thread tags such as unseen, ignored and watched, which has served me well for many years.

I run an external synchronization script to send and receive mails with the following tools: msmtp, mbsync, sieve-filter and notmuch new. I then read, tag and compose mails directly within Emacs.

Upgrading to Emacs 30

For my latest setup I upgraded to the upcoming Emacs 30. I wanted to explore the new defaults, which includes enhanced tree-sitter modes and a new project--remember-dir function for dynamically recording new projects.

Here is how I built Emacs from source: 

dnf config-manager --enable codeready-builder-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms
dnf install -y texinfo zlib-devel libgccjit-devel ncurses-devel gnutls-devel
git clone --depth 1 -b emacs-30 https://git.savannah.gnu.org/git/emacs.git && cd emacs
./autogen.sh
./configure --prefix=/usr/local/emacs --without-all --with-x-toolkit=no --with-native-compilation --with-gpm --with-zlib --enable-link-time-optimization --with-gnutls
make && sudo make install

During this transition, I encountered a couple of issues with my config, something that’s to be expected with unreleased software:

  • Ivy completion in shell mode drops the previous path segment: swiper#3051.

  • Org element may now be lazy, causing my org-next-schedule to require manual forcing of headlines: org-ql#364.

While these errors were somewhat frustrating, I was able to quickly identify the root cause and implement workarounds. Given that Emacs is 40 years old, it’s impressive how well Elisp code has stood the test of time.

Alternatives

I find Emacs to be significantly ahead of the competition, particularly when evaluated against the following criteria:

  • Is it a free software that I can modify?
  • Is it portable and lightweight?
  • Is it stable?

While I appreciate alternatives like Vim or Acme, I find Emacs to be simpler and more integrated. However, I also believe that a fully integrated system can be preferable in certain scenarios. For instance, I wouldn’t mind using:

  • Pharo for Smalltalk.
  • Eclipse for Java.
  • Visual studio for Windows.

Conclusion

In this post I focused on the core features of Emacs that I rely on for my work. I had to skip some of the additional functionalities you might expect from a text editor, such as: spell checkers, abbreviations, Dired, Info and Tramp.

My goal is to inspire you to give Emacs a try. If you decide to dive in, here are some tips to enhance your keyboard ergonomics:

  • Adopt the default keybindings, perhaps with an home row mod to reduce strain on your pinkies.
  • Consider the evil package to get the vim modal editing.
  • Explore alternatives like meow or boon for different keybinding schemes.

Lastly, Emacs is perfectly suited for integrating AI workflow, and you’ll be able to implement the fanciest demo if you are into that sort of things. One of my colleagues even wrote the allow-lists-for-ai-services package to prevent leaking private data, and as far I can tell, this only exists in Emacs. I personally don’t use AI services out of ethical concern and I’m satisfied with good old-fashioned local completion that doesn’t boil the ocean.

Thanks for your time!

item.title: Diabetes Cure: Scientists Close to Creating 'Simple Pill'
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @amichail
December 14, 2024 | https://weblo.info/scientists-close-to-creating-simple-pill-diabetes/ | archive.org

Researchers at Mount Sinai have uncovered a groundbreaking method that could transform diabetes care forever. This discovery could lead to a simple pill capable of reprogramming the body to produce insulin, offering hope to over 500 million people worldwide living with diabetes.

Dr. Esra Karakose, a lead researcher at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, emphasized the revolutionary potential of this approach:

“This is an exciting finding that shows harmine-family drugs may be able to induce lineage conversion in human pancreatic islets.”

The Problem: A Global Diabetes Epidemic

Diabetes affects 537 million people globally, with both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes stemming from the inability of pancreatic beta cells to produce insulin. Current treatments manage symptoms but don’t restore the body’s ability to produce insulin. Researchers have long searched for ways to regenerate or replenish these critical beta cells.

A Breakthrough Years in the Making

Mount Sinai’s journey began in 2015 when researchers discovered harmine, a DYRK1A inhibitor capable of stimulating beta cell regeneration. Since then, the team has advanced the science, demonstrating in 2019 and 2020 that harmine works synergistically with GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide and exenatide to enhance beta cell regeneration.

In July 2024, researchers reported astonishing results:

  • Harmine alone increased human beta cell mass by 300%.
  • When combined with a GLP-1 receptor agonist, the increase soared to 700%.

An Unexpected Reservoir of Potential

The most exciting discovery? Alpha cells, another type of pancreatic cell, may hold the key to creating new beta cells. These alpha cells are abundant in diabetic patients and could be reprogrammed to produce insulin.

Using single-cell RNA sequencing technology, researchers analyzed over 109,881 individual cells from pancreatic islets donated by adults. They identified “cycling alpha cells,” which demonstrated potential to transform into beta cells.

“It may mean that people with all forms of diabetes have a large potential ‘reservoir’ for future beta cells, just waiting to be activated by drugs like harmine,” said Dr. Karakose.

How It Works: The Science Behind the Pill

The research focused on stimulating alpha cells to take on beta cell characteristics. The team observed that small-molecule drugs increased the number of cycling alpha cells while triggering them to produce insulin-related markers.

The findings suggest that, with the right drugs, alpha cells could replenish beta cells—potentially eliminating the need for insulin injections.

Challenges and Limitations

While the results are promising, the study is still in its early stages:

  • The sample size was small, involving only four donors.
  • Experiments were conducted in a lab setting, not in living humans.
  • The long-term stability of newly formed beta cells remains unconfirmed.

Despite these challenges, researchers are optimistic about the next steps, including human trials.

What’s Next? Moving Toward Human Trials

Mount Sinai researchers are working to translate their findings into a treatment accessible to millions. Combining harmine with a GLP-1 receptor agonist could pave the way for a scalable, affordable pill.

Dr. Andrew F. Stewart, director of the Mount Sinai Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism Institute, remarked:
“A simple pill, perhaps together with a GLP1RA like semaglutide, is affordable and scalable to the millions of people with diabetes.”

A Revolutionary Shift in Diabetes Care

If successful, this approach could:

  • Restore natural insulin production.
  • Eliminate the need for daily injections.
  • Offer a simpler, more effective treatment for both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.

This breakthrough represents not just a scientific achievement but a beacon of hope for millions managing diabetes.

Call to Action

Stay updated on this revolutionary research as Mount Sinai continues to push boundaries. For more information, visit Mount Sinai Diabetes Research. Share this story to spread hope and awareness about this potential game-changer in diabetes care.

This article was crafted based on the latest research published in Cell Reports Medicine and reflects the collaborative efforts of Mount Sinai’s esteemed team of scientists.

item.title: In Search of a Faster SQLite
item.description:
Score 9 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @avinassh
December 14, 2024 | https://avi.im/blag/2024/faster-sqlite/ | archive.org

SQLite is already fast. But can we make it even faster? Researchers at the University of Helsinki and Cambridge began with this question and published a paper, “Serverless Runtime / Database Co-Design With Asynchronous I/O”. They demonstrate up to a 100x reduction in tail latency. These are my notes on the paper.

This is the foundational paper behind Limbo, the SQLite rewrite in Rust. Let’s dive in.

Note that this is a workshop paper and a very short read. It also focuses more on serverless and edge computing. However, the learnings here can be applied more broadly.

tl;dr Using asynchronous I/O and storage disaggregation can make SQLite faster.

io_uring

There are two things I really loved in this paper: their explanation of query execution and how io_uring works.

The io_uring subsystem in the Linux kernel provides an interface for asynchronous I/O. Its name has its roots in the ring buffers shared between user space and kernel space that alleviate the overheads of copying buffers between them [3]. It allows the application to submit an I/O request and concurrently perform other tasks until it receives a notification from the OS on the com- pletion of the I/O operation.

With io_uring, the application first calls the io_uring_setup() system call to set up two memory regions: the submission and completion queues. The applications then submit I/O requests to the submission queue and call the io_uring_enter() system call to tell the OS to start processing the I/O requests. However, unlike the blocking read() and write()calls, io_uring_enter() does not block the thread by returning control to the userspace. The application can now perform other work concurrently and periodically poll the completion queue in userspace for I/O completion.

They also detail how SQLite executes a query, which is relevant later:

An application first opens a database with the sqlite3_open() function. As SQLite uses files for storing the data, the sqlite3_open() function invokes the low level OS I/O, such as POSIX open, for opening the file. The application then prepares a SQL statement using the sqlite3_prepare() function that transforms SQL statements such as SELECT and INSERT into sequences of bytecode instructions. The application then executes the statement with the sqlite3_step() function.

The sqlite3_step() function executes the sequence of bytecode instructions until the query produces a row to read, or it com- pletes. When there is a row, the function returns the SQLITE_ROW value and when the statement is complete, the function returns SQLITE_DONE. The sqlite3_step() function internally calls into the backend pager, traversing the database B-trees representing tables and rows. If a B-Tree page is not in the SQLite page cache, the page has to be read from disk. SQLite uses synchronous I/O such as the read system call in POSIX to read the page contents from disk to memory, which means the sqlite3_step() function blocks the kernel thread, requiring applications to utilize more threads to perform work concurrently to the I/O wait.

The Premise

The first part of the paper discusses the rise of serverless compute and its benefits. One problem in such runtimes is database latency. Imagine your app runs at the edge, but the database resides in a cloud environment. Your serverless function incurs the cost of network round trips between the serverless function and the cloud.

One solution is colocating the data at the edge itself. But a better approach is a database embedded in the edge runtime itself. With this, database latency becomes zero. This is the holy grail. This slaps.

Cloudflare Workers already achieves this but exposes a KV interface. However, the authors argue that KV doesn’t suit all problem domains. Mapping table-like data into a KV model leads to poor developer experience and (de)serialization costs. SQL would be much better, and SQLite being embedded solves this—it can be directly embedded in the serverless runtime.

SQLite uses synchronous I/O. The traditional POSIX I/O system calls read() and write() block the thread until I/O is complete. While this is fine for smaller apps, it becomes a bottleneck when running hundreds of SQLite databases on a server. Maximizing resource usage is crucial.

SQLite comes with its own issues: concurrency and multi-tenancy. Since I/O is synchronous, thus blocking, this makes applications running on the machine compete for resources. This also increases latency.

Why can’t we just move SQLite to io_uring?

Replacing the POSIX I/O calls with io_uring is not trivial, and applications that use blocking I/O must be re-designed for the asynchronous I/O model of io_uring. Specifically, applications now need to handle the situation of I/O submission in their control flow. In the case of SQLite, the library needs to return control to the application when I/O is in flight.

In other words, you need to rewrite much of SQLite. The researchers chose a different approach: rewrite SQLite in Rust using io_uring.

Limbo

They modify the VM and BTree components to support async I/O, replacing sync bytecode instructions with async counterparts:

Let’s take one instruction: What does Next do? It advances the cursor and (may) fetch the next page. When it’s doing disk I/O, it is blocked. The DB issues a Next call to the VM, and it’s blocked until the page is retrieved from the disk and returned to the caller.

In the async version, first NextAsync is submitted and immediately returned. Now the caller can block or do other operations. Async I/O removes blocking and improves concurrency. Here is the bytecode comparison of both:

However, to maximize resource usage, they propose one more thing: decoupling query and storage engines i.e. Disaggregated Storage. I have written about it explaining the basics here - Disaggregated Storage - a brief introduction

Evaluation and Results

For benchmarking, they simulate a multi-tenant serverless runtime, where each tenant gets their own embedded database. They vary the number of tenants from 1 to 100 in increments of 10. SQLite gets its own thread per tenant, and in each thread they run the query to measure. Then they run SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100 SQL query 1000 times. For Limbo, they do the same but use Rust coroutines.

The results show a remarkable 100x reduction in tail latency at p999. They also observe that SQLite query latency does not degrade gracefully with the number of threads.

(orange is limbo) graph showing the latency degradation of SQLite. Smaller is better.

The work is very much in progress, and the paper leaves a couple of questions unanswered. They address these in the Future Work section where they mention doing more benchmarks with multiple readers and writers. The benefits become noticeable only at p999 onwards; for p90 and p99, the performance is almost the same as SQLite. (Could it be because they run a single query?)

The Limbo code is open source: https://github.com/tursodatabase/limbo

Limbo is now an official Turso project and here is the announcement post.

item.title: We've Been Here Before
item.description:
Score 3 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @thunderbong
December 14, 2024 | https://terriblesoftware.org/2024/12/14/weve-been-here-before/ | archive.org

“Humans are allergic to change“ — Grace Hopper

In the late 1950s, a new programming language called COBOL emerged with a bold premise: it would enable people without traditional programming backgrounds — business professionals, managers, and analysts — to directly write and understand code. Its syntax was designed to be as close to English as possible, so that non-developers could, in theory, specify instructions for the computer.

Many experienced programmers of the time found this idea unsettling. If anyone could now “program” in this new language, what would become of them? (If there had been social media back then, we’d have seen those “PROGRAMMING IS DEAD” posts popping up everywhere.)

And yet, COBOL (and similar languages) didn’t eliminate the need for programmers. In fact, it only increased it. Rather than spending all day handling low-level machine code, these engineers could focus on bigger-picture problems. Instead of taking their jobs, it made them more productive.

You see, these programmers quickly realized that their job wasn’t just to type on the keyboard or implement the same low-level algorithms again and again. They saw that their job was to ship working software that adds real value to users.

COBOL is just one example. Don’t even get me started on Object-Oriented Programming or Low Code/No Code platforms — every time these “threats” showed up, people worried the need for skilled engineers would vanish. But guess what? It never happened.

You’re probably seeing where I’m going with this, but yeah: AI. Just as these earlier waves of change never replaced the human element in engineering, AI won’t either. By offloading repetitive tasks, AI frees us to focus on what matters most: understanding user needs, making smart product decisions, and delivering real value — faster than ever.

It’s worth repeating: the heart of our profession isn’t in typing lines of code; it’s in shipping software that truly helps people.

We’ve seen this pattern before, and we’ll see it again. New tools change the landscape, but they don’t diminish the role of the human mind. Our capacity to think critically, empathize with users, and create working solutions will always remain essential — no matter how advanced our tools become.
